title: Designing healthcare for people and planet: What if every act of care also cared for the planet?
acknowledgements: Aws Almukhtar, Daniella Watson, Jessica Newberry Le Vay, Leila Shepherd, Matt Harrison, and Natalia Kurek
short_description: This blog explores how healthcare can be designed to reduce its environmental impact, setting out six areas where design can help the NHS cut waste and emissions while improving care.
lay_summary:
Healthcare contributes to climate change, but it can also be part of the solution. In the UK, the NHS accounts for around 4 to 5 per cent of the country's total carbon emissions. At the same time, climate change is making people ill through heatwaves, floods and worsening air quality. This creates a double challenge: health systems need to reduce their own environmental footprint while also preparing for rising demand.

This blog, written by Helix Centre designers Sophie Horrocks and Tori Simpson, sets out six areas where design can help. These are: reducing clinical waste, making care pathways more sustainable, greening digital health technologies, designing hospital buildings for a low-carbon future, shifting care into communities, and embedding sustainability into policy and everyday practice.

For each area, the authors describe the problem, share examples of work already underway, and point to sessions at the World Design Congress where these ideas were being explored further. The examples range from a behavioural "nudge" tested by Helix to reduce unnecessary glove use on hospital wards (which led to an 11 per cent improvement in hand hygiene compliance), to the NHS's first zero-emissions ambulance being trialled in the West Midlands, to solar panels at Milton Keynes University Hospital generating around 8 per cent of the site's electricity.

The blog also highlights tensions that need to be navigated. For example, digital tools can cut travel and improve efficiency, but data centres use large amounts of energy and water. Reusable medical equipment can reduce waste, but sterilising it is sometimes as carbon-intensive as replacing it. And while moving care into communities can lower emissions, it must be done in ways that do not leave people behind.

The authors argue that sustainability should not feel like an extra burden for already stretched health services. Instead, there are "win-wins" to be found, where greener choices also improve care, save money, or support staff wellbeing. They invite designers, clinicians and partners to join the conversation and help shape healthcare that protects both people and the planet.

title: Monitoring night-time safety in households with dementia using ambient sensing technologies: a rule-based decision algorithm
authors: Alina-Irina Serban, Sophie Horrocks, Chloe Walsh, Matthew Harrison, Eyal Soreq, Amer Marzuki, Mark Woodbridge, Ramin Nilforooshan, Rafael A Calvo, David J Sharp
short_description: Researchers developed and tested a system that uses sensors in the home to detect when a person with dementia leaves the house or opens a door at night, so that family carers can be alerted to potential safety risks.
lay_summary:
Wandering at night is common among people living with dementia, affecting around 6 in 10 people as the condition progresses. It can put people at risk of falls, getting lost, or being outside in unsafe conditions, and it adds to the strain on family members and carers. Despite how often it happens, there are few reliable tools to help spot these risks early.

A team led by the UK Dementia Research Institute's Care Research and Technology centre, with design expertise from the Helix Centre, developed a monitoring system to address this. The system uses sensors placed around the home: motion detectors, door sensors, and a mat placed under the mattress that tracks whether someone is in bed. An automated algorithm analyses the data from these sensors to identify patterns that might signal a safety concern, such as leaving the house during the night or leaving a door open.

The algorithm was tested in stages, including trials in a living lab (a test home set up for research), computer simulations, and real-world use. The main validation involved 94 households monitored over 365 nights, totalling nearly 300,000 hours of data. In 33 of those households, at least one night-time safety alert was triggered. Across all households, the system generated 200 alerts over 142 nights. When someone did go out at night, they were outside for an average of 2 hours and 40 minutes per event.

Of the alerts, about 9 in 10 were confirmed as genuine night-time outings. Around 15% of those turned out to be routine activities rather than risky events, which is a useful reminder that not every alert means something is wrong.

This was a validation study, not a trial of whether the system improves outcomes for people with dementia or their carers. The authors note that the system has the potential to improve safety and reduce carer burden, but further research would be needed to test that in practice. The study also relied on sensor data rather than direct observation, so some events may have been missed or misclassified.

title: Remote detection of Alzheimer's disease pathology using a digital sleep and circadian biomarker: an InSleep46 study
authors: Josh King-Robson, Eyal Soreq, Molly R E Cartlidge, Matthew Harrison, Heidi Murray-Smith, Lina Aimola, Marie Poole, Ríona Mc Ardle, Ashvini Keshavan, David M Cash, William Coath, Louise Robinson, David J Sharp, Jonathan M Schott
short_description: Researchers tested whether a sleep sensor placed under the mattress at home could detect early signs of Alzheimer's disease in people with no symptoms, and found it performed as well as a blood test at identifying those with significant brain changes.
lay_summary:
Detecting Alzheimer's disease before symptoms appear could open the door to earlier treatment, but current methods (brain scans and blood tests) are expensive or require a clinic visit. This study asked whether patterns in sleep and body rhythms, collected at home using a simple sensor, could flag people at higher risk.

The research was led by teams at UCL, the UK Dementia Research Institute Care Research & Technology Centre at Imperial College London, and Newcastle University, as part of the Insight 46 study. Helix designed the participant experience, making it possible for over 250 people in their late 70s to install the sleep sensors themselves at home. Helix also led focus groups with a diverse group of participants to explore how acceptable this kind of monitoring felt.

Participants were all born in March 1946 and had already taken part in brain scans and blood tests as part of the wider study. At around age 78, they were sent a thin sensor to place under their mattress. The device recorded sleep stages, heart rate, breathing rate, snoring and time spent awake each night, without the person having to do anything. In total, the team collected data from over 63,000 nights of sleep (about 174 years' worth), with each participant contributing an average of 240 nights.

The researchers built a computer model to see whether these sleep patterns could predict who had a build-up of tau protein in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer's. The model performed well for people with more advanced tau deposits (Braak stage 3 or higher), achieving an accuracy score comparable to a blood test for phosphorylated tau (pTau217). It was less effective at picking up earlier stages of the disease or amyloid protein alone.

This is a proof-of-concept study, not a finished screening tool. The participants were all the same age and from a single birth cohort, so the findings need to be tested in other groups. The team is now working to refine the model, confirm the results elsewhere, and find out how many nights of recording are needed for a reliable prediction.

If the approach holds up, it could offer a low-cost, low-burden way to identify people who might benefit from further testing or future treatments, all from data collected while they sleep.
diagram_caption: Diagram showing the process or recruitment, data collection and analysis.

title: InSleep46: Designing future dementia care through sleep data
authors: Sophie Horrocks, Ríona McArdle, Marie Poole, Josh King-Robson, Jonathan Schott, David Sharp, Matthew Harrison, Louise Robinson
short_description: The InSleep46 project explored how under-mattress sleep sensors might support earlier detection, diagnosis and care for dementia, using co-design workshops and interviews to understand what would make such technology acceptable, useful and fair.
lay_summary:
Around 900,000 people in the UK live with dementia, and that number is expected to rise. Research suggests that changes in sleep may signal early shifts in brain health, sometimes before memory problems appear. Passive sleep sensors, placed under the mattress and requiring no daily interaction, offer a low-burden way to track these changes at home.

The InSleep46 project set out to explore whether this technology could play a role in dementia prevention, diagnosis or ongoing care. The project brought together researchers from Imperial College London, University College London, Newcastle University and the Helix Centre. Alongside a scientific study collecting sleep data from over 250 members of a long-running UK birth cohort, the Helix Centre and Newcastle University led the human-factors research: understanding how people affected by dementia, members of the public and GPs feel about using sleep sensors in real life.

The team ran three co-design workshops in London and Newcastle with 31 members of the public, aged 31 to 82, who brought a range of perspectives including personal and caregiving experience of dementia. They also interviewed seven GPs. Participants discussed whether the technology felt acceptable, what support they would need to use it confidently, and what concerns it raised.

Many people welcomed the idea of an early warning tool, particularly when framed around "brain health" rather than dementia risk. But they also raised concerns: anxiety about unclear results, the risk of widening health inequalities if only affluent or tech-savvy people could access the sensors, and the need for clear next steps rather than data without action. GPs highlighted limited time in consultations and a lack of training to interpret sleep data, and wanted strong evidence before adopting new tools.

Using these insights, the team developed three speculative service scenarios: one focused on prevention (sensors offered through pharmacies to encourage healthy sleep habits), one on diagnosis (sensors used alongside other tests when someone has memory or sleep concerns), and one on monitoring (sensors supporting ongoing care for people already diagnosed). These scenarios were tested with the wider project team, whose expertise spans clinical practice, data science, health inequalities and lived experience.

The findings highlight that trust, equity and clear clinical pathways will be essential if sleep-sensing technology is to work in practice. Future research should validate the link between sleep patterns and dementia risk, explore emotional impacts, and ensure that any service reaches people who might benefit most, not only those already engaged with health technology.

title: End User and Primary Care Physicians’ Perspectives on Digital Innovations in Dementia Risk Detection: Focus on a Digital Sleep Biomarker
authors: Ríona McArdle, Marie Poole, Sophie Horrocks, Josh King-Robson, Jonathan Schott, David Sharp, Matthew Harrison, Louise Robinson
short_description: Researchers asked members of the public and GPs what they thought about using a digital sleep mat to help spot early signs of dementia risk, and found that while the public were generally open to the idea, GPs wanted stronger evidence and clearer guidance before they would use it in practice.
lay_summary:
Sleep problems are common in people with dementia and may appear before memory symptoms do. This has led researchers to ask whether tracking sleep patterns could help identify people at higher risk of developing dementia. A team led by Newcastle University, in collaboration with Imperial College London and UCL, explored what members of the public and GPs think about using a digital sleep mat for this purpose. The Helix Centre at Imperial contributed co-design and public involvement expertise to the project.

The sleep mat sits under the mattress and records sleep patterns over three months. From this data, researchers can calculate a score (called the DRI-SI) that may indicate dementia risk. The team wanted to understand whether people would be willing to use the mat at home, and whether GPs would feel comfortable offering it as part of NHS care.

Thirty-one members of the public took part in focus groups in Newcastle and London. All had some connection to dementia, either through their own concerns, a family history, or experience as a carer. Seven GPs from across England were interviewed separately.

The public were generally positive. They found the mat unobtrusive and liked the idea of catching problems early. Their concerns were practical: how to set it up, who would pay for it, and whether factors like a restless partner or getting up in the night might affect the results. Some worried about data privacy, particularly if commercial companies were involved.

GPs were more cautious. They wanted to see published evidence that the sleep score is accurate and that acting on it would genuinely help patients. Without clear guidance on what to do with a high-risk result, they worried about causing anxiety without being able to offer a next step. They also raised concerns about adding to their workload when primary care is already stretched.

The study highlights a gap between public enthusiasm and clinical readiness. The authors suggest that integrating the sleep mat into specialist brain health clinics, rather than general practice, might be a useful next step. This would allow further research while keeping the tool within a clinical setting where follow-up support is available.

The findings offer five recommendations for anyone developing digital tools to detect dementia risk: train clinical staff on the science behind the tool; make sure the technology is easy to use for everyone; be clear about how the tool has been tested and validated; present results in a way that is meaningful to patients and clinicians; and be transparent about how data is stored and used.

title: Designing for healthy ageing: Lessons learned from engaging pre-frail older adults in the development of digital self-monitoring health technologies
authors: Alex Dallman-Porter, Tori Simpson, Andrew Watt, Tricia Tay, Souradip Mookerjee, Shuang Wu, Gianpaolo Fusari, Matthew Harrison, David Sunkersing, Kate Grailey, Jonathan J Gregory, Michael Fertleman, Ara Darzi, Leila Shepherd
acknowledgements: Helix Centre team (including Damion Lambert, Brian Quan); Clinical Reference Group (including Simon Dryden, Hutan Ashrafian, Sabaa Gauhar, Ana Luísa Neves, Brendan Delaney, Alison Buttenheim, Louis Koizia, Cerys Morgan, George Peck, Melanie Dani); Helix interns (Madeline Tatum, Jessica Shields).
short_description: Thirty older adults tested a home health-monitoring system using smartwatches, passive sensors, and an our Healthy Habits app. While most found the technology easy to use and were happy to have the system in their homes for extended periods, when it came to interacting with the app many only glanced at their data without acting on it, pointing to a need for clearer, more personalised guidance.
lay_summary:
People are living longer than previous generations, but the extra years are not always healthy ones. Frailty, a gradual loss of strength and energy, becomes more common with age. Catching this early, at the "pre-frail" stage, gives the best chance of slowing or reversing it through exercise and lifestyle changes. Wearable devices and health apps could help people track their activity and sleep at home, but older adults have been slower to adopt these tools than younger groups. This study set out to understand why, and to learn how such technology could be designed to work better for them.

Thirty people aged 65 and over, all living independently in London and showing early signs of frailty, took part. Each received a smartwatch, a sleep sensor placed under the mattress, and small sensors around the home, along with a tablet app that displayed their data and offered tips for staying active. Participants used the system for at least six weeks, and most chose to continue longer (the average was about seven months). The research team visited regularly and collected feedback through questionnaires and conversations.

Most participants found the equipment unobtrusive and were comfortable having sensors in their homes. Nearly 8 in 10 chose to extend their time in the study, and the overall feedback was positive. However, the way people engaged with their data was often shallow: they would check their daily step count or sleep score but rarely look at trends over time or set goals. Several factors contributed to this. Some joined out of curiosity rather than a firm intention to change habits. Others worried about pressing the wrong button or "breaking" something. Many felt the advice was too generic, or doubted the accuracy of the readings.Participants said they would value more human guidance, such as a conversation with a professional who could explain what the numbers meant and suggest realistic next steps. At the same time, they disliked being "nagged" by automated reminders, highlighting a tricky balance for designers: people want support, but also want to feel in control.

The study has limitations. Participants were recruited in London and tended to be relatively confident with technology, so the findings may not apply to less digitally experienced groups. Feedback was captured in notes rather than full transcripts, which may have introduced some bias. The authors suggest that future versions of this kind of system could use conversational AI to give people a more natural way to ask questions and receive tailored explanations, though more research is needed on how to do this safely and effectively for older adults.
diagram_caption: Selected screens from the Healthy Habits app: goal setting, overview of steps data, detailed historical steps data, and information on why the habit 'steps' is important. The same views are available across 4 'healthy habits': Steps, Sleep, Sedentary Time, and Active Minutes.

title: Head-to-Head: A Comparative Validation of Ubiquitous Gait Sensing Approaches for Frailty Detection in Older Adults
authors: Shuang Wu, Alex Dallman-Porter, Souradip Mookerjee, Shruthi K. Hiremath, & Katrin Hänsel
acknowledgements: Tis study is supported by Optum. We would also like to thank the Imperial College Biodynamics Lab for allowing us the use of their equipment and for their generous help in carrying the testing and processing the data.
short_description: Researchers compared four types of sensor (radar, motion sensors, a back-worn accelerometer and a smartwatch) to find out which could most accurately and acceptably measure walking speed at home, as a way to spot early signs of frailty in older adults.
lay_summary:
Walking speed is sometimes called "the sixth vital sign" because it is closely linked to health in later life. A slowing gait can be an early sign of frailty, a state of reduced physical reserve that makes people more vulnerable to falls, illness and loss of independence. Spotting frailty early could allow people to take action before problems become serious, but current assessments happen mainly in clinics and often only after someone is already quite frail. Continuous monitoring at home might catch changes sooner, yet until now there has been no direct comparison of the different sensors that could do this job.

This study tested four sensors head to head: a small radar unit, a pair of passive infrared motion detectors (the kind used in home security systems), an accelerometer worn on the lower back, and a consumer smartwatch worn on the wrist. The work began with a workshop involving 14 older adults, who handled each device and gave their views on comfort, ease of setup and usefulness. The smartwatch was the clear favourite; participants valued its familiarity and extra features. A common concern across all sensors was whether they would capture enough data to be meaningful.

The sensors were then tested in two controlled settings. First, 14 older adults walked up and down an office corridor while all four sensors recorded at once, with a stopwatch providing the reference measurement. All sensors except the radar mounted sideways achieved acceptable accuracy, with errors below the 0.2 metres per second threshold considered clinically important. Second, 23 older adults repeated the exercise in a specialist gait laboratory equipped with a motion capture system (the gold standard for measuring movement). Early analysis suggests the radar may actually track moment-to-moment changes in speed more faithfully than the other sensors, which tend to produce a single average figure.

The next phase, an eight-week study with 50 older adults using all four sensors in their own homes, is due to begin in late 2026, subject to ethics approval. This will test how well the sensors perform in everyday life, where people walk in different directions, at different times, and without a set distance.

The findings so far show that several low-cost, unobtrusive sensors can measure walking speed accurately enough to be useful, and that older adults are willing to use them. The study also highlights that the way accuracy is judged matters: a stopwatch gives only an average, while radar captures the natural variation in how people walk, which may turn out to be more informative for detecting early frailty.

title: Patient experiences of waiting for orthopaedic care and priorities for ‘waiting well’: a qualitative study in a London NHS trust
theme: Imperial College NHS Trust Improvement Work
authors: Jodie Chan, Sharon Poon, Anna Lawrence-Jones, Fiona O'Driscoll, Carol Waugh, Abiola Awojobi-Johnson, Leila Shepherd, Kate Grailey
acknowledgements: The research team would like to thank the Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust Business Intelligence and Orthopaedics teams for their support in carrying out the study. We would also like to thank Mieko Wertheim for her support and guidance as a public partner.
keywords: Public and Patient Involvement and Engagement (PPIE)
short_description: Patients waiting for orthopaedic surgery in a London NHS trust described how long waits affected their pain, mobility, independence and mental wellbeing, and worked with researchers to design support ideas such as regular check-in messages and peer-written information.
lay_summary:
NHS waiting lists have grown sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic, and people living in more deprived areas tend to wait longer and be hit harder by the effects. This study set out to understand what it is like to wait for orthopaedic treatment (such as a hip or knee replacement) and what would help people live well while they wait.

The research team interviewed seven patients living in the most deprived areas of North West London who had waited, or were still waiting, more than 18 weeks for an orthopaedic procedure. Two public partners with their own experience of waiting helped shape the questions, analyse the findings and run a later workshop. A further six patients took part in that workshop, where they turned the interview findings into practical ideas for support.

Patients described immediate effects of waiting: ongoing pain, difficulty with everyday tasks such as shopping or climbing stairs, greater reliance on family and friends, and anxiety about when treatment would come. When waits stretched on or appointments were cancelled at short notice, the effects deepened. Some people's conditions got worse, life plans such as weddings or holidays were put on hold, hope faded, and trust in the NHS fell. Those with caring responsibilities or less support at home were particularly affected.

When asked what would help, patients focused less on lifestyle advice and more on being kept informed and feeling acknowledged. They wanted honest estimates of how long they would wait, regular updates so they did not feel forgotten, and a way to speak to someone in the orthopaedics service when they had questions.

At the workshop, patients developed four ideas: a check-in text, letter or phone call every few months to acknowledge the wait and point people to support; a letter written by past patients explaining how physiotherapy had helped them; a booklet of coping tips suggested by other patients; and training for staff to help them understand the wider impact of waiting.

This was a small, exploratory study at a single site, so the findings should be seen as a starting point. No Asian patients took part despite being invited, and some people dropped out because of pain or other commitments, which may have shaped the results. Even so, the themes were consistent across interviews, and the ideas generated offer a practical foundation for services looking to support patients better while they wait.

title: UPBEAT Trial: a randomised feasibility evaluation of a digital system for UPper limB rEhabilitation After sTroke
authors: Gianpaolo Fusari, Sarah Coleman, Jane Davies, Jeremy Dearling, Joanne Findlay, Mark Goddard, Nicola Ivins, Fiona Jones, Fiona Leggat, Rachel Lowe, Clare McCrudden, Richard McKinlay, Ebenezar Ndachi Effiang, Louise Penny, Rebecca Playle, Davina Richardson, Muhammad Riaz, Leila Shepherd, Tongtong Shi, Tomasz Szymanski & Ara Darzi
acknowledgements: The authors would like to thank all patients and clinicians for their participation in this research. The authors also acknowledge the contributions of the PPIE and Trial Steering Committee groups, as well as those of all therapy teams at ICHT, CLCH and HRCH.
short_description: A feasibility trial found that OnTrack, a wearable digital system for arm rehabilitation after stroke, can be delivered within NHS stroke services, with strong patient engagement and high acceptability.
lay_summary:
Many people who survive a stroke struggle to regain use of their arm. Although rehabilitation can help, NHS services often cannot provide enough therapy to meet demand. OnTrack is a digital tool designed to help stroke survivors practise arm movements on their own, between formal therapy sessions. It uses a smartwatch to track arm activity and provides real-time feedback, alongside coaching from a therapist trained in self-management support. The system was developed with stroke survivors, carers and therapists.

This study tested whether OnTrack could be delivered in NHS stroke services and whether a larger trial would be practical. Thirty stroke survivors with arm weakness took part, recruited from one hospital and two community rehabilitation teams in London. Half received OnTrack alongside their usual care, and half received usual care alone. Participants were followed up at 6 and 12 weeks.

The trial met most of its targets. Eighty percent of participants completed the study, and those using OnTrack engaged with it on average 6.3 days per week, a high level of adherence. Participants rated the system as easy to use. Trends in the data suggested improvements in arm function and confidence in both groups, though the study was not designed to measure effectiveness. The cost of delivering OnTrack was estimated at around £1,500 per patient, and the methods for collecting health and cost data worked well.

Some areas need improvement before a larger trial. Recruitment was slower than hoped, and the way therapists delivered the coaching was inconsistent, suggesting that training needs to be strengthened. The study also found that participants in the usual care group were more likely to drop out, which is a common challenge in rehabilitation trials.

Overall, the findings support the case for a full-scale trial. Digital tools like OnTrack may offer a practical way to help stroke survivors get more rehabilitation practice, addressing a gap in current NHS services.

title: What is the feasibility and patient acceptability of a digital system for arm and hand rehabilitation after stroke? A mixed-methods, single-arm feasibility study of the ‘OnTrack’ intervention for hospital and home use
authors: Gianpaolo Fusari, Ella Gibbs, Lily Hoskin, Anna Lawrence-­ Jones, Daniel Dickens, Roberto Fernandez Crespo, Melanie Leis, Jennifer Crow, Elizabeth Taylor, Fiona Jones, Ara Darzi
acknowledgements: The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of all the members of the PPI group; all participants involved; Peter Wilding, Meenakshi Nayar and Davina Richardson and therapy teams at ICHT; therapy teams at CLCH; Ruth Nicholson for her support in ethics applications and procedures; Steve McAteer and Eleni Daniels for their guidance on the BRC program; Dr Hendramoorthy Maheswaran for his help reviewing the manuscript.
short_description: This feasibility study tested OnTrack, a digital system combining a smartwatch and coaching to help people use their affected arm more after a stroke, and found it was acceptable to participants and ready for a larger trial.
lay_summary:
Arm weakness is one of the most common effects of stroke, affecting around 450,000 people in the UK. Recovery depends on repetitive activity, but many people struggle to know what to do, how much to do, and whether they are making progress. Once they leave hospital, stroke survivors often feel unsupported and unsure how to help themselves.

OnTrack is a digital system designed to address this. It combines a smartwatch worn on the affected arm (which tracks how much the arm is moving), a smartphone app that shows progress and sends motivational messages, and regular one-to-one coaching sessions to help people set goals and build self-management skills. The aim is to give people the feedback and support they need to practise independently, alongside their usual NHS rehabilitation.

This study tested whether OnTrack was practical to deliver and acceptable to the people using it. Twenty-four adults who had had a stroke in the previous six months were recruited from NHS stroke services in North West London. Twelve completed the full 12-week programme. The study ran partly before and partly during the COVID-19 pandemic, which meant some participants used OnTrack at home with remote coaching rather than starting in hospital.

Participants wore the smartwatch on about six days out of seven and checked their activity data regularly. On average, they increased their arm activity by 63% over the 12 weeks. In interviews, they said the activity targets were motivating and the coaching was a valuable part of the experience. Therapists involved in recruitment felt the study procedures were manageable and that OnTrack could help people engage more with their recovery.

The study was not designed to prove that OnTrack improves arm function (that would need a larger randomised trial), but it showed that recruitment, retention and completion rates were acceptable, and it identified suitable outcome measures and sample sizes for a future trial. The authors note that the messaging part of the system received mixed feedback and needs further refinement, and that questions remain about how coaching could be delivered at scale. A patient and public involvement group contributed throughout, helping to refine the intervention and interpret the findings.

title: Is a novel digital system for arm and hand rehabilitation suitable for stroke survivors? A qualitative process evaluation of OnTrack
authors: Elizabeth Taylor, Gianpaolo Fusari, Ara Darzi, Fiona Jones
acknowledgements: The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of all the members of the PPI group and all participants involved, as well as the therapists who helped with recruitment of participants, and all those involved in the OnTrack study.
short_description: This qualitative study explored how stroke survivors experienced OnTrack, a digital arm rehabilitation programme combining activity tracking, coaching and messaging, and found that participants valued the whole package but placed particular importance on the human support from coaches.
lay_summary:
Arm weakness affects around 450,000 people who have a stroke in the UK each year. Recovery depends on regular, repetitive practice, but many stroke survivors feel unsupported after leaving hospital and unsure how to continue improving on their own. OnTrack is a 12-week programme designed to help. It combines a wrist-worn tracker that measures arm movement, a smartphone app that shows progress and sends motivational messages, and regular one-to-one coaching sessions focused on self-management.

This study sat alongside a feasibility trial of OnTrack (reported separately) and aimed to understand how participants experienced the programme and whether it was delivered as intended. Eleven people who had completed OnTrack were interviewed, and seven coaching sessions were observed by researchers independent of the delivery team. A group of stroke survivors also helped analyse the interview data halfway through the study, and their feedback led to changes in how coaching was delivered.

Participants said they valued the programme as a whole, not just one part of it. However, the human element stood out. People spoke warmly about their coaches, describing them as kind, approachable and good listeners. They appreciated the regular check-ins and the encouragement to keep going, as well as the understanding shown on difficult days. The coaching sessions were adapted during the study to focus more on activities that mattered to each person (such as buttering toast or opening jars) rather than just numerical movement targets.

Views on the motivational messages were more mixed. Some people found them helpful, especially when they included tips or links to useful information. Others found generic encouragement irritating and wanted messages to feel more personal. Participants generally found the activity tracking motivating, though some noticed that a busy day did not always show up as high arm activity, and that tracked movement was not always the same as useful movement.

Most participants felt confident they could continue practising independently after the programme ended, though some said they would have liked a follow-up check-in. The study was affected by COVID-19, which meant some coaching moved online, but participants found remote sessions acceptable.

The authors note that only people who completed the programme were interviewed, so the views of those who dropped out are not included. They also highlight that the coaches in this study were researchers with a deep understanding of the programme, and further work is needed to understand what training others would need to deliver OnTrack effectively.

title: Feedback from wearable devices accelerates recovery after breast cancer surgery
authors: Ahmed Latif, Noer Al Janabi, Meera Joshi, Nur Amalina Che Bakri, Richard M. Kwasnicki, Gianpaolo Fusari, Leila Shepherd, Ara Darzi, Daniel R. Leff
acknowledgements: We thank the patients and staff at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and Imperial College London, for their support. This study was funded by Imperial College London MedTechOne and the Wellcome Trust. Infrastructure support for this research was provided by the NIHR Imperial Biomedical Research Centre (BRC). We gratefully acknowledge their support, which made this work possible.
short_description: This study found that breast cancer patients who received personalised, clinician-guided feedback from a wearable device recovered arm movement faster after surgery than those with fixed goals or no feedback, suggesting wearables could help fill gaps in post-operative rehabilitation.
lay_summary:
Surgery to the armpit (axilla) is a common part of breast cancer treatment, but it often leaves people with shoulder stiffness, weakness or reduced arm movement. Structured physiotherapy can help, but access is inconsistent: many patients receive only a leaflet or brief advice rather than ongoing support. This study tested whether a smartwatch paired with a rehabilitation app could help people recover arm function more quickly after surgery.

Forty-nine women took part. Twenty wore an Apple Watch running OnTrack, an app originally developed at the Helix Centre for stroke rehabilitation and adapted here for breast cancer. The app tracks how much the arm moves, displays progress towards a daily goal, and sends motivational messages. Half of these participants were given a fixed target of 60 minutes of arm movement per day (basic feedback). The other half had their targets adjusted weekly by a clinician based on how they were progressing (dynamic feedback). A further 29 patients from an earlier study at the same hospital, who wore a passive movement sensor with no feedback, served as a comparison group.

Participants wore the watch for at least a week before surgery to establish their normal activity level, then continued wearing it for up to 16 weeks afterwards. Adherence was high: on average, people used the system on nearly 9 out of every 10 days, and usability scores were very positive.

The results showed clear differences between groups. By day 8 after surgery, patients receiving dynamic feedback had returned to their pre-surgery activity levels (on average, 103% of baseline), while those with basic feedback were at 80% and those with no feedback at 86%. The dynamic-feedback group also reached a stable recovery point earlier (day 4, compared with day 5 for basic feedback and day 7 for no feedback). When the researchers looked only at patients who had the less extensive sentinel lymph node biopsy (rather than full lymph node removal), the pattern held: dynamic feedback still outperformed no feedback.

The study has limitations. The sample was small, and the comparison group came from an earlier time period using a different device, which makes direct comparison harder. Most participants had early-stage disease treated with breast-conserving surgery, so the findings may not apply to those having mastectomy or more extensive lymph node removal. The researchers also note that the system measured overall arm movement rather than specific exercises, and that patient-reported outcomes (such as pain and function questionnaires) did not show a clear link with the activity data, possibly because the questionnaires were collected weeks after the main recovery differences appeared.

The authors conclude that wearable-guided rehabilitation with personalised, clinician-adjusted goals shows promise for accelerating recovery after breast cancer surgery. Larger randomised trials are now needed to confirm these findings and assess long-term benefits and cost-effectiveness.

title: Use of commercially available wearable devices for physical rehabilitation in healthcare: a systematic review
authors: Ahmed Latif, Hasaneen Fathy Al Janabi, Meera Joshi, Gianpaolo Fusari, Leila Shepherd, Ara Darzi, Daniel R Leff
acknowledgements: The authors thank the medical librarians at St Mary’s Hospital, London, who contributed to the systematic review search strategy.
short_description: This systematic review found that consumer-grade wearable devices such as Fitbits and Apple Watches can support physical rehabilitation after surgery or stroke, with some trials suggesting they may work as well as traditional physiotherapy for certain patients.
lay_summary:
Physiotherapy is essential for recovery after events such as surgery or stroke, but access is often limited by long waiting times and a shortage of staff. Wearable devices (smartwatches and fitness trackers that people can buy off the shelf) offer a possible way to support patients in managing their own rehabilitation at home. This review, led by Imperial College London with academic input from the Helix Centre, set out to examine whether these devices actually improve recovery, and to map which devices are being used and in which areas of medicine.

The researchers searched four major databases and identified 18 studies, covering 1,754 patients in total. Six were randomised controlled trials (the most reliable type of study) and 12 were smaller observational or feasibility studies. The studies spanned orthopaedics (mainly hip and knee replacements), stroke medicine, cancer care and general surgery. The most commonly used device was the Fitbit, followed by Apple Watch and iPhone combinations. Step count was the most frequent measure of physical activity.

All six randomised trials found that patients who received feedback from a wearable device were more physically active than those who did not. Two orthopaedic trials went further, showing that patients using a smartwatch-based rehabilitation app achieved similar outcomes to those receiving traditional face-to-face physiotherapy, with fewer clinic visits. The smaller, non-randomised studies consistently found that wearable-supported rehabilitation was feasible and acceptable to patients.

The authors note several limitations. Most studies were small, follow-up periods were short (the longest was 12 months), and some excluded patients who did not own a compatible smartphone, which could bias results towards people already comfortable with technology. There were no randomised trials in cancer care, and the stroke studies tended to include only patients with mild impairments, so findings may not apply to everyone. The review also highlights that economic evaluations are lacking: before wearables can be recommended widely, we need to know whether they save money as well as time.

The review concludes that consumer-grade wearables show promise as additions to, or in some cases alternatives to, traditional physiotherapy for people recovering from surgery or stroke. However, larger and better-designed trials, along with cost-effectiveness analyses, are needed before they can be adopted routinely in healthcare.

title: Virtual reality for acute pain in outpatient hysteroscopy: a randomised controlled trial
authors: N Deo, KS Khan, J Mak, J Allotey, FJ Gonzalez Carreras, G Fusari, J Benn
acknowledgements: We thank all the women who consented to participate in the trial as well as all nurses and gynaecologists who performed the procedure: their enthusiasm and support as co-researchers in this clinical project was indispensable. A special thanks for Jayshree Patel and Chris Astley, the lovely couple who helped co-design the study and gave a patient’s perspective along with technical expertise. We are grateful to Dr Sheila Popert, Medical Director at St Giles Hospice, for commissioning the video and requesting David Attenborough to lend his voice for the narration in the Video ‘Forest of Serenity’, which was the centre stone for the intervention. We are indebted to Anna Wojdecka, Visiting Lecturer, Healthcare & Design at the Royal College of Art, London, for providing design ideas and academic rigour in the conduct of this study.
short_description: This randomised trial found that women who used a virtual reality headset during outpatient hysteroscopy experienced significantly less pain and anxiety than those receiving standard care, suggesting VR could be a useful addition to pain management in clinic-based gynaecological procedures.
lay_summary:
Outpatient hysteroscopy (a procedure to examine the inside of the womb using a small camera) is increasingly carried out in clinic rather than under general anaesthetic. While most women tolerate it well, some experience significant pain and anxiety. Current options for pain relief include local anaesthetic and simple painkillers, but there is no strong consensus on what works best.

This study, conducted as part of a Healthcare and Design Masters project with academic supervision from the Helix Centre, tested whether virtual reality could help. Forty women scheduled for outpatient hysteroscopy at a London hospital were randomly assigned to either standard care or to wear a VR headset during the procedure. The headset showed an eight-minute calming video called "Forest of Serenity", featuring a rainforest and lake scene narrated by Sir David Attenborough. Women could look around the virtual environment by moving their head.

Women in the VR group reported substantially lower pain and anxiety scores. Average pain was 38% lower (3.7 out of 10 compared with 6.0), worst pain was 28% lower, and anxiety was 39% lower. These differences remained after adjusting for factors such as whether women had given birth before or had gone through the menopause. All women in the VR group said they would be happy to have the procedure in the outpatient setting again, compared with 85% of those receiving standard care.

Interviews with participants suggested that the VR worked by creating a sense of relaxation and distraction. Some women appreciated that the headset blocked their view of the clinical equipment. A small number found the headset uncomfortable or felt mildly nauseous, and one woman with a history of claustrophobia removed it, but most found it acceptable. Clinical staff reported that the intervention was feasible and helpful in the majority of cases.

The authors note several limitations. The study was small (40 women), and because participants knew whether they were using VR, there may have been some placebo effect. The video was filmed from a standing perspective rather than lying down, which limited how much of the virtual environment could be explored. For two women, the procedure lasted longer than the video, requiring it to be restarted.

The researchers conclude that VR is a promising, non-drug option for managing pain and anxiety during outpatient gynaecological procedures. Larger trials and economic evaluations are needed before it could be adopted routinely.
